samples.text:
The chart shows how many passengers used six international airports in 2019 and in 2023.

Airport A was the busiest airport in both years. It had 86 million passengers in 2019, but in 2023 it decreased to 79 million. Airport B was second, and it increased from 71 million to 76 million, so the difference between A and B become smaller.

Airport C had 64 million passengers in 2019, but it fell to 51 million in 2023, which is the biggest decrease in the chart. Because of this, Airport D which increased from 48 million to 52 million was a little higher than Airport C in 2023.

The two smaller airports was different. Airport E went down from 35 million to 25 million, however Airport F went up from 22 million to 29 million. So Airport F was still the smallest but it was closer to Airport E than before.

Overall, three airports had less passengers in 2023 than in 2019 and three airports had more. Airport A was the busiest and Airport F was the least busy in both years.
samples.why: Figures accurate and key changes noted · overview present but basic and placed last · linking adequate but mechanical · some repetition · agreement, tense, quantifier and punctuation errors that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
The bar chart compares passenger numbers at six international airports in 2019 and 2023.

Overall, half of the airports handled fewer passengers in 2023 than in 2019, while the other half saw an increase. Airport A remained the busiest airport throughout, and Airport F the least busy.

Airport A served 86 million passengers in 2019, but this figure fell to 79 million in 2023. Meanwhile, Airport B grew from 71 million to 76 million, which reduced the gap between the two largest airports from 15 million to only 3 million. Airport C experienced the sharpest drop, losing 13 million passengers to finish at 51 million, and as a result it was narrowly overtaken by Airport D, whose passenger numbers rose modestly from 48 million to 52 million.

Among the smaller airports, the trends were opposite. Airport E saw its passengers fall from 35 million to 25 million, whereas Airport F recorded the largest increase of any airport, going up by 7 million to 29 million. Consequently, the difference between these two airports were much smaller in 2023, at just 4 million.
samples.why: Clear overview of rises and falls · key features highlighted, including changes in ranking · logical organisation with good cohesive devices · appropriate vocabulary · mostly accurate with one agreement slip.

samples.text:
The chart compares the number of passengers passing through six international airports in 2019 and 2023.

The six airports were split evenly between those that gained and those that lost passengers over the period. Although Airport A retained its position as the busiest and Airport F remained the quietest, the gaps between several airports narrowed noticeably.

Airport A handled 86 million passengers in 2019, 15 million more than Airport B. By 2023, however, its total had slipped to 79 million, whereas Airport B had grown to 76 million, leaving the two almost level. Airport C suffered the steepest decline of all, from 64 million to 51 million, and was consequently overtaken, albeit narrowly, by Airport D, which rose from 48 million to 52 million.

A similar contrast can be seen between the two smallest airports. Passenger numbers at Airport E fell by more than a quarter, from 35 million to 25 million, whereas Airport F grew by almost a third, from 22 million to 29 million, the largest increase recorded. As a result, Airport F ended the period only 4 million passengers behind Airport E.
samples.why: Key features skilfully selected, including narrowing gaps and ranking changes · clear overview · accurate derived comparisons · cohesion managed well · precise vocabulary · varied, error-free structures.
